source: Klayman & Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing
finding: The 'confirmation bias' in the 2-4-6 task is better described as a general positive test strategy: test cases you expect to fit your hypothesis. The paper says the tendency is widely replicated and is not a bad heuristic in general. It fails when the hypothesis is narrower than the true rule, as in Wason's task.
numbers: Theory paper with a probabilistic model; cites replications by Mynatt et al. 1977/78, Tweney et al. 1980, Gorman & Gorman 1984, Taplin 1975, Mahoney 1976/79. Doherty & Falgout: 32 of 40 data-saving patterns were positive-test patterns.
quote: the +test strategy leads people to perform tests of both sufficiency and necessity
limits: Positive testing is fine when the hypothesis is about as broad as the target and targets are rare. Negative tests are needed when H is a strict subset of the true rule. A surprising verification of a long-shot hypothesis can carry more information than an expected falsification.
agent_relevance: Do not force negative tests everywhere. S4 should pick the test type by the relation between hypothesis and the plausible rule set: probe outside the hypothesis when it may be too narrow. This refines G3.

source: Klayman & Ha (1987), section on Tweney et al. (1980) DAX/MED feedback
finding: Giving feedback as DAX (the rule) and MED (everything else) made solvers treat the two as two hypotheses and test each with positive tests, which tests the complement. This greatly improved success. More test opportunities and less time pressure also made people test more widely.
numbers: Described as the one manipulation that 'greatly improved success'. DAX/MED solvers used even fewer pure negative tests than usual, yet solved more.
limits: Mechanism is two complementary hypotheses, not more negative tests as such. Exact rates are in Tweney et al. (1980), not opened.
agent_relevance: Cheap scaffold trick: state the complement (rule R and not-R) and test both with ordinary positive tests. This is the Dual-Goal idea later used as an LLM prompt.

source: Gale & Ball (2002) Does positivity bias explain patterns of performance on Wason's 2-4-6 task?
finding: A 2x2 design separated number of goals (one vs two complementary) from feedback labels (DAX/MED vs fits/does not fit). The Dual-Goal advantage appeared with both label types, which supports goal complementarity over a positivity-bias account. Producing at least one negative triple was most strongly tied to success.
numbers: Standard-task success about 20%; Dual-Goal at least double. Only the abstract page was opened: sample size and test statistics not available.
quote: producing at least one negative triple is most closely associated with success
limits: Conference proceeding, not refereed per the repository record. Rival accounts: Evans (1989) positivity bias vs Wharton, Cheng & Wickens (1993) goal complementarity.
agent_relevance: Two explicit goals (find the rule, find the complement) are the active ingredient. Build a 'what would the opposite rule predict' slot into S4.

source: Gorman & Gorman (1984) A comparison of disconfirmatory, confirmatory and control strategies on Wason's 2-4-6 task
finding: Telling individuals to use a disconfirmatory strategy made them solve the 2-4-6 problem significantly more often than confirmatory or no-strategy groups, and they obtained more falsifying information. Earlier individual-subject studies had mostly found no gain from telling people to falsify.
numbers: Three conditions (confirmatory, disconfirmatory, control). Abstract page only: N and success rates not stated there.
limits: Boundary condition proposed by the authors: the gain appears when subjects get no feedback on their rule guesses until the end. Earlier null results gave immediate feedback.
agent_relevance: A plain 'try to falsify' instruction can work, but depends on how the loop gives feedback. Keep guess feedback away from the test-selection step.

source: Branchini, Burro, Bianchi (2023) Training People to Think in Opposites Facilitates the Falsification Process in Wason's Rule Discovery Task
finding: A short 'think in opposites' training raised 2-4-6 success from 36.66% to 78.33%. Trained solvers found the rule on the first announcement far more often (57.4% of their correct solutions vs 13.63% in control). Training made each solution slower.
numbers: N=120 adults, random assignment to training or control. chi2(1)=22.067, p<.001, R2=0.178. 47 correct in training, 22 in control. Time to solution F(1,67)=10.63, p=.002 (slower with training). Control correct solutions: 13.63% first attempt, 45.45% second, 40.90% third.
quote: Thinking in opposites nearly doubled the success rate
limits: One lab, Italian adult sample, one task. Standard 2-4-6 with three announcement attempts. The training is about contrast, not the word 'falsify'.
agent_relevance: Origin of the Think-in-Opposites prompt used in LLM work. A concrete operation ('pick a property, test its opposite') beats 'be skeptical'. Candidate wording for S4.

source: Branchini et al. (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing performance in Wason's rule-discovery task, Memory & Cognition
finding: A three-arm follow-up shows the opposites step is the active part. Listing the properties of the seed triple alone did nothing; listing properties and then their opposites nearly doubled success. The gain came from less repetition of the same hypothesis and more awareness of the ascending-descending dimension, not from more tests.
numbers: N=180. Success 78.33% (opposites), 38.33% (properties only), 36.66% (control). chi2(2)=27.986, p<.001. Time to solution F(2,89)=6.541, p=.002 (slower in both training arms). Attempt of solution F(2,89)=5.702, p=.004. A priori power analysis: 78 needed.
limits: Same lab as the 2023 study, so not an independent replication. Interpreted as counterfactual thinking (iterative counterfactual model).
agent_relevance: A structured analysis without the opposite step does nothing. The scaffold must include the explicit opposite or complement step, not just a request to analyse.

source: Berthet et al. (2024) A common factor underlying individual differences in confirmation bias, Scientific Reports
finding: Across three adapted paradigms (Wason selection task, 2-4-6 task, interviewee task) people chose confirming over disconfirming options, and bias scores converge across paradigms more within a component than within a paradigm. Information search showed the largest effect. Search bias correlated with lower cognitive ability and lower CRT.
numbers: N=200. Confirming 69.1% vs disconfirming 48.2%, F(1,198)=158.12, d=0.89. Search d=1.18, weighing d=0.31, memory d=0.59. Logical-rule d=0.72, numerical-rule d=0.91, trait d=0.36. Best CFA fit chi2(15)=21.76, CFI=.981, RMSEA=.047. Subsample N=107: information search vs cognitive ability r=-.35, vs CRT r=-.34, vs pseudoscientific beliefs r=.20.
limits: Six of nine measures reached alpha >= .69; trait tasks had low reliability (.48 to .69). Trait paradigm showed no bias in weighing or memory. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Bias in search is the largest and most stable component and tracks reasoning ability, which fits the LLM result that stronger reasoning models show less of it. Put the guard at test selection.

source: Executive learning and the Wason selection task, PLoS One (2015), 'Helping reasoners succeed in the Wason selection task: when executive learning discourages ...'
finding: On a rule falsification task before training, 39 of 42 participants answered incorrectly, mostly by matching the named items (34 of 39). After executive learning (practising inhibition of the matching response), logical responses on the selection task rose from 0% to 26.6%.
numbers: Pre-test: 3 of 42 logical on the rule falsification task. Post-test logical answers 26.6% after executive learning vs 0% before (Fisher exact p=.02). Group difference chi2(2)=7.92, p=.02.
limits: Small groups; most answers stayed non-logical after training. Transfer shown for the executive-learning group, not the logical-learning group.
agent_relevance: Surface matching is hard to remove by teaching logic; practice at inhibiting the first response transfers. Suggests the program should block the first-instinct test, not only explain falsification.

source: Ragni, Kola, Johnson-Laird (2018) On selecting evidence to test hypotheses: A theory of selection tasks (via search summary)
finding: Meta-analysis of 228 selection-task experiments. Selections were more redundant than 10,000 simulated independent selections in 99 experiments. A dual-process model-theory algorithm fit best and the authors say it eliminated all but one of 15 rival theories. Kellen & Klauer criticised the model selection as non-identifiable.
numbers: 228 experiments; 99 with redundant selections. Figures from a search summary, not read in full.
limits: Contested: Kellen & Klauer dispute the analysis; Ragni & Johnson-Laird replied. Search summary also says another meta-analysis finds the falsifying card is the one most often overlooked.
agent_relevance: Rival theories (matching, rational analysis, model theory) disagree on why the falsifying card is skipped. Do not build the agent on one account.

source: Scheel, Schijen, Lakens (2021) An excess of positive results: Comparing the standard psychology literature with Registered Reports (via search summary)
finding: Only 44% of first hypotheses in Registered Reports found support, against 96% in the standard literature. With direct replications removed the gap stays near 96% vs 50%. At community level, falsification is lost when failed tests go unpublished.
numbers: 71 Registered Reports (as of Nov 2018) vs a random sample of 152 standard hypothesis-testing papers. 96% vs 44%; 96% vs 50% without direct replications.
limits: Observational comparison; authors say it does not show Registered Reports reduce bias. Summary from search result, full text blocked.
agent_relevance: A log of failed tests inside the agent plays the role of a registered report: commit to the test before seeing its result and keep refutations.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Across eleven LLMs, models propose triples that fit their own hypothesis and so discover the 2-4-6 rule slowly or never. The ratio of incompatible to compatible tests (I:C) correlates positively with success, as in human data. Two debiasing prompts raise success: Think-in-Opposites in every setting and Dual-Goal in eight of eleven.
numbers: Success from 6% (Qwen3-8B non-thinking) to 78% (Gemini-2.5-Pro with Dual-Goal or Think-in-Opposites), turn limit 45, 80 episodes per model-variant. Average discovery rises from 42% to 56% with interventions. Gemini-2.5-Pro baseline 0.73, I:C 0.66. Thinking Qwen3-8B baseline 0.21, I:C 0.15. Human reference (Wason 1960): 29 people, 21 solved, I:C 1.79 for first-try correct vs 0.24 for first-try wrong.
quote: confirmation bias manifests not in how evidence is interpreted, but in how evidence is selected
limits: Synthetic rule sets, one task family. Effects significant for thinking models, mixed for non-thinking. Switching to thinking mode raised success without consistently raising I:C, so the two are not the same thing.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3 and for a test-selection prompt in S4. Also a warning: Dual-Goal can hurt non-reasoning models, so measure before shipping.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (distillation and transfer)
finding: Fine-tuning students on traces made under the Think-in-Opposites prompt raised success without the prompt, and part of the effect transferred to a different hypothesis-testing task, the Blicket test. A small student distilled from a larger teacher with the prompt did best.
numbers: Qwen3-8B thinking: baseline 0.21 success, I:C 0.15; with TiO teacher 0.36. Qwen3-32B baseline 0.41, TiO 0.61. Cross-scale plus intervention distillation (8B student from 32B with TiO): 0.59 success, I:C 0.38. Paper text: 'almost tripling the task success rates'.
limits: Distillation set built from the same Wason task family; Blicket transfer called promising, not complete. Table layout partly garbled in extracted text, so only values stated clearly are used.
agent_relevance: The gain is not just prompt wording, but our agent is a scaffold with no training, so the prompt route is the relevant one.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: A semantic version of 2-4-6 with 12 LLMs: reasoning models beat instruction-tuned models, and the main driver of success is negative testing (testing outside the current hypothesis). No model comes close to optimal.
numbers: Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33 to 35%, GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Spearman rho between positive-test share and success -0.779 (p=0.003). Positive-test share: GPT-5-Mini 39.0%, GPT-5.2-Chat 27.3%, GPT-OSS-20B 24.2% vs 66 to 82% for instruction-tuned. 100 games per model.
limits: Small reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano, Qwen3.5-9B) did worse than instruction-tuned models, so extended thinking alone does not help at small scale. Each model also served as oracle (accuracy 85 to 95% for most).
agent_relevance: Confirms on a new task and new models that falsifying probes drive success. Gives a metric: share of tests outside the hypothesis per run. Small-model caveat matters for a nano agent.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games (regression and turn-level analysis)
finding: A mixed-effects logistic regression over 1,200 games shows confirmation bias strongly predicts failure while oracle error does not. Turn-level labelling shows negative tests give conclusive falsifications much more often.
numbers: Bayesian mixed-effects logistic, n=1,200 games: confirmation bias posterior mean -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error -0.12 (OR 0.885, interval spans zero). Conclusive falsification rate GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%. Spearman between bias and conclusive falsification -0.937 (p<0.001).
limits: Hypothesis-target relations were labelled by GPT-5-Mini. Oracle error was checked by a human on one test and one guess per game only. In partial-overlap or disjoint cases positive tests can falsify too; the subset case dominated (over 50% of turns for most models).
agent_relevance: Matches Klayman & Ha: negative tests matter when the hypothesis is too narrow. S4 should ask whether H is a subset of what could be true, then probe outside it.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games (failure beyond confirmation bias)
finding: Failed games contained more turns where the hypothesis was disjoint from or only partly overlapping the target, meaning the model did not follow a clear path from narrow to broad. Raw oracle quality did not explain success.
numbers: Oracle Cohen's kappa ranges from 0.34 (Mistral-Small-24B, guess turns) to 0.98 (GPT-5.2-Chat). MiniMax-M2.5, GLM-5 and GPT-5-Nano had similar oracle scores yet won 35%, 58% and 12% of games.
limits: Semantic category games (WordNet), 20-turn limit; may not carry to numeric rules.
agent_relevance: Bad hypothesis moves, not only bad tests, cause failure. Pair the test rule with a rule that the next hypothesis must be a revision of the last.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: An early LLM version of 2-4-6 (Boolean rule over three numbers, up to 30 tests). All tested models do badly. A common failure is confirmation bias: testing only the first plausible rule. Stronger models more often try to falsify.
numbers: 50 tasks per model. Accuracy: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28%), o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, chatgpt-4o-latest 11/50, Mistral Large 2 11/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Llama 3.1 405B 8/50, GPT-4o-mini 6/50, Gemini 1.5 Pro 5/50. Avg guesses: o1-preview 12.1, GPT-4o 26.56. Avg repeated tests: GPT-4o-mini 9.78, GPT-4o 2.84, o1-preview 0.06.
quote: Stronger models will more explicitly attempt to falsify these hypotheses instead.
limits: Only 50 tasks per model, 2024 models, no explicit confirmation-bias metric. Reasoning models guessed early and gathered too little evidence, so they lost to Sonnet 3.5 despite better deduction.
agent_relevance: Gathering evidence and deducing from it are separate skills. The program should enforce a minimum number of distinct tests before a final guess.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT, appendix B.3 example of an o1-preview failure
finding: o1-preview failed a relatively easy rule because it latched on to an early observed behaviour (the rule returns true when all three values are equal), submitted five of nine tests confirming it and none exploring other cases.
numbers: 9 tests used, 5 confirming it, most of the test budget left unused.
limits: Single anecdote, not a rate.
agent_relevance: Concrete failure pattern for an S4 guard: if several consecutive tests agree with H, the next test must come from outside H.

source: Batista & Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
finding: In a preregistered human experiment where a chatbot supplied 2-4-6 examples, default GPT-5.1 behaved like confirming-only evidence: low rule discovery and rising confidence. Unbiased random examples from the true rule gave about five times the discovery rate. A Bayesian fed hypothesis-sampled data gains confidence without moving toward the truth.
numbers: N=557 (Prolific), 504 in discovery analysis. Discovery: Random Sequence 29.5%, Rule Disconfirming 14.1%, Agreeable 11.8%, Rule Confirming 8.4%, Default GPT 5.9%. chi2(4)=28.02, p<.001. Default vs Disconfirming p=.043. Default vs Random 23.6 pp, p<.001. Confidence change: Rule Confirming +9.5 vs Rule Disconfirming -20.6 (d=1.04); Default GPT +5.4; Default vs Random d=1.92. TOST: Default and Rule Confirming equivalent within 0.5 SD.
quote: Unmodified LLM behavior suppressed discovery and inflated confidence
limits: One model, one task, human participants. Confirming vs Disconfirming discovery difference not significant (p=.143). Why the default model samples confirmingly is left open.
agent_relevance: Evidence sampled from the agent's own hypothesis is not independent evidence. Test generators should sample from a spread of alternatives, not from H. Relevant to self-generated tests under G3.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? Evaluating Algorithmic Reasoning with Counterexample Creation (REFUTE)
finding: LLMs that can solve competitive programming problems are far worse at finding a counterexample to a subtly wrong solution. The gap persists with code execution and even when the correct solution is given.
numbers: 324 problems. Best model o3-mini (high) creates counterexamples for under 9% of incorrect solutions yet is rated to solve about 48.7% of the problems from scratch (DeepSeek-R1 44.0%). Random-search strategy: 35% of samples end with an incorrect counterexample; of those 14% fail test validation and 86% have wrong brute-force code. o3-mini random search invalidated 6% extra distinct submissions that other strategies missed.
quote: even OpenAI o3-mini (high) with code execution feedback, can create counterexamples for only < 9% of incorrect solutions
limits: Algorithmic domain where counterexamples are code-checkable; early 2025 models. Table 1 cells garbled in extraction, headline figures from abstract and text.
agent_relevance: Falsifying is harder than generating. A scaffold should not assume the model can think of a refuting case; give it a checkable generator (random input plus brute-force check).

source: Huang, Jin, Li, Li, Candes, Leskovec (2025) Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (POPPER)
finding: An agent design built on falsification: one agent proposes measurable implications of a hypothesis as null-hypothesis tests, another runs them, and e-values are combined sequentially so Type-I error stays controlled. It had the highest power among methods that also controlled error.
numbers: Alpha=0.1, 5 runs. DiscoveryBench: 66.5% more power than ReAct; TargetVal-IL2: 3.17 times the power of Self-Refine. Most baselines failed to control Type-I error; removing the relevance checker raised it. Human study, 9 computational biologists: no significant difference in error or power, POPPER 9.7x faster, 3.6x more lines of code, 2.5x more statistical tests.
limits: Negative controls made by column permutation; expert study small (9 people, one benchmark). The LLM relevance checker agreed with humans at Spearman 0.55 and overrated relevance (85% vs 77% human pass rate).
agent_relevance: Most direct use of Popper in an LLM agent. What separates it from ReAct and Self-Refine is principled evidence accumulation. A nano agent can borrow the idea of a sequential evidence ledger without e-values.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER, error analysis and backbone choice
finding: Top failure reasons were misreading p-values and weak test design, not hallucination. The backbone mattered: Claude Haiku 3.5 had a high Type-I error while Llama 3.3 70B, GPT-4o, Sonnet 3.5 and o1 kept reasonable error control.
numbers: Failure shares: misinterpreted p-values 35.9%, ineffective falsification design 28.1%, falsification test breaks implication 17.2%, incorrect implementation 8.6%, hallucination 0.8%.
limits: Error categories assigned by an LLM then checked by humans. Per-model table cells garbled in extraction, so numeric Type-I values are not reproduced.
agent_relevance: A model that cannot design a test that truly follows from H will not falsify well. In a small-model agent, a check that the test really follows from H matters more than adding more tests.

source: P-Bench and Fisher-R1 (2026) Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
finding: On 425 open-ended hypothesis-testing tasks with audited p-values, strong agents often make inferential errors. RL with a statistical reward improved a 14B open model past larger systems.
numbers: P-Bench: 425 tasks (203 easy, 222 hard). Strict pass@1 hard: GPT-5.4 30.5%, DeepSeek V4 Pro 26.3%, Fisher-R1-14B 33.0%. Easy strict: GPT-5.4 64.7%, Fisher-R1-14B 64.2%. Training: 8,642 synthetic tasks over 27 methods.
limits: Summary page only. Tests statistical validity of a run test, not whether the agent chose a falsifying test.
agent_relevance: Even after a test is chosen, running it correctly is a separate failure point. Code-check the statistical step.

source: Wikipedia, Wason selection task (review page)
finding: Review page says fewer than 10% of people gave the correct falsifying selection (the 8 and the red card) in Wason's four-card task and that it was replicated in 1993. A study of 112 people found performance on evolutionarily familiar versions relates more to general intelligence than performance on novel ones.
numbers: Under 10% correct (Wason 1977 as cited). Evans, Newstead & Byrne 1993 replication, no figures given. Kaufman et al. (2011): N=112, 70-item computerised Cosmides-Tooby task, no coefficient given.
limits: Secondary encyclopedia source with no meta-analytic numbers. The familiar drinking-age version is easy for most people, so failure depends on abstract content.
agent_relevance: The same logic problem becomes easy with familiar content, so S4 tests should be framed in the concrete domain of the task, not abstractly.

source: Tweney et al. (1980) Strategies of rule discovery in an inference task (via Gale & Ball page and search summary)
finding: Search summary reports the Dual-Goal (DAX/MED) version of 2-4-6 gave about 60% first-announcement success and was replicated many times; the standard task is commonly about 20%.
numbers: About 60% vs about 20%. The Gale & Ball page confirms 'at least double' and about 20%.
limits: Original not opened; the 60% figure is from a secondary summary.
agent_relevance: A framing change alone can triple human success, so framing is a cheap lever for the agent.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task, as summarised in Jhaveri et al. (2026)
finding: Founding result seen through the 2026 paper: 29 people, 21 eventually found the correct rule, 6 on the first announcement. First-announcement correct solvers tested more incompatible triples than first-announcement wrong ones.
numbers: N=29; 21 solved; 6 correct at first announcement; I:C 1.79 for first-correct vs 0.24 for first-incorrect; second-announcement correct 0.50 vs 0.19. Session limit 45 minutes.
limits: Second-hand through a 2026 summary. Tiny sample, and the target rule 'any increasing sequence' is unusually broad, which Klayman & Ha show makes positive testing fail.
agent_relevance: Human baseline to compare an LLM I:C ratio against.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026): interventions on non-reasoning models (boundary condition)
finding: Interventions that help thinking models can fail for models without reasoning traces. Dual-Goal lowered success for non-thinking Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B and was flat for Llama-3.3-70B.
numbers: Non-thinking success, baseline / Think-in-Opposites / Dual-Goal: Qwen3-14B 0.23 / 0.29 / 0.13; Qwen3-32B 0.33 / 0.36 / 0.10; GPT-4o 0.11 / 0.16 / 0.14; Llama-3.3-70B 0.21 / 0.38 / 0.20. Significant gains for thinking models only.
limits: Cells read from a table with partly garbled layout, paired by row order and checked against the paper's text that Think-in-Opposites improved success in all scenarios.
agent_relevance: A nano model without a long reasoning trace may be hurt by a complex dual-goal prompt. Prefer the simple 'test the opposite of one property' step and measure it.
